utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Are there any preliminary matters? I see you on your feet, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, only briefly, and that relates to a document that is P2361 in evidence in this case. We've identified an administrative error that was made with respect to this document, and the document bears the -- should have borne the ERN 0434-0857. Inadvertently, the document that was up-loaded had the ERN 0454-0857, and so we'd like to replace the document that's in evidence with the proper document which was admitted pursuant to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This correction is appreciated. You should replace the correct -- the incorrect document by the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If there's nothing else, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Janc. Welcome back. You know the affirmation to tell the truth you made yesterday -- you made at the beginning of your testimony last year still applies. Mr. Vanderpuye is continuing his examination-in-chief. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, and good afternoon to you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone, and to you, Mr. Janc. Before we continue with the questioning, Mr. President, I mentioned yesterday that I would tender the documents that I used last with Mr. Janc before we broke. Those were 65 ter numbers 5408, 5611, and 7452.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The document 65 ter 7452 was not included into the 65 ter exhibit list, and, therefore, I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir if you have any objection to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list and if you have any objection to the request of the Prosecution to tender these three documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I hope this day will end in accordance with God's will. I do not object to any of the documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter 7452 should be added to the 65 ter exhibit list. All three documents mentioned by Mr. Vanderpuye will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 5408 shall be assigned Exhibit P2449. 65 ter document number 5611 shall be assigned Exhibit P2450.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. The next one should only be marked for identification, pending translation. We don't have a translation yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I refer to 65 ter 7452.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And 65 ter document number 7452 shall be assigned Exhibit P2451, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. If I could refer the Chamber to tab number 5 and have in e-court, please, 65 ter 5544 [Realtime transcript read in error "5554"]. We have a different intercept in the English. It should be 9 October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But while that's coming up, let me ask you, Mr. Janc: Did you have a chance to review this intercept, that is 9 October 1994, 1905 hours?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to able to find any material or review any material supporting the content or reliability of this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is only one document, and this is an intercept from the BiH State -- SDB, actually, about the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We'll note in this context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have the right one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's still not the right one in B/C/S. It should be ERN 0415-0603. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to this intercept, we can see it indicates that this is a transcript of a conversation between an interpreter, Svetlana, between General Briquemont and General Mladic. Were you able to confirm that in the SDB -- Bosnian SDB intercept that you compared this one to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 3, line 13, it says "5554." I think this document has a different number, 5544. At least that's what it says on my list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you are perfectly correct. Thank you for this correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, are you able to answer the last question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My answer would be, yes, that's correct, this information is contained in the SDB intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this particular conversation, we can see what the topic of it is. Could you tell us, were you able to confirm the entirety of this conversation, part of the conversation? What about it were you able to confirm in the SDB intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire conversation is also included there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 5612. This may be a little tricky. What I'd like to do is to put them side by side, but obviously I don't believe we can have the interpretations up at the same time as well. So let's first look at the intercept, and then we can try that. So we'll look at 5612, 65 ter 5612, and then we can compare it, after we've done that, to the 65 ter 5544.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, Mr. Janc, is this the intercept you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we can see that this refers to a conversation on 9 October 1994. The time indicated in this intercept is about 1915 hours?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, which is slightly different than from the Croatian intercept, where we have the time at 1905.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we can see here, as has been General Tolimir's concern with respect to these intercepts, that it says: "Translation from English." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to this intercept, is your explanation or view as to why that appears in this document the same as it was with respect to the other MUP SDB intercepts we've seen so far or is it different?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would say it's the same, because in every single one -- single intercept, we can see, at the beginning, the sentence that one of those UNPROFOR members is talking through interpreter with someone from the VRS side. So the explanation would be the same for all those three intercepts from the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the Croatian intercept, we don't have it on the screen, but you may recall there's a reference here to an interpreter named Svetlana. Have you come across that name, in looking at any of the intercept evidence in this case, as an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, this name is quite familiar to me. Of course, I came across this name reviewing the intercepts; not only the Croatian intercepts, but also the intercepts which were intercepted by the BiH. Especially, I think there are some intercepts between General Gvero and some of the UNPROFOR members, I think General Nicolai talking to General Gvero through Interpreter Svetlana.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to this intercept, this is the one we have on the screen now, the SDB -- Sector SDB Sarajevo intercept, did you see that -- if there were any discrepancies between this intercept, that is, in terms of its content, and the Croatian intercept that we looked at before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. I think they are quite the same, so I don't see any big discrepancies. I would need to go carefully through them again, but I think that both of them would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, what I'd like to do is, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, is to put these two intercepts up next to each other. I think we'll have to do it in the English first, and then if there are any questions that arise from that, then we can look at it also in B/C/S to see if there is any significant difference between them. So if we could, I'd like to have 65 ter 5544, which is the Croatian intercept, on the left side, and 5612 on the right side, and perhaps we can go through it quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have it on the screen, both in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can see here, Mr. Janc, clearly, that the dates are the same, and as you've indicated previously, the times of the intercept are 1905 and 1915 respectively. And, once again, we can see that there is a conversation between General Mladic and General Briquemont. But we can see, in the Croatian intercept, an indication that the interpreter here is someone by the name of Svetlana, and we see, in the MUP SDB intercept, that it is a female interpreter or there is a female interpreter. As you go through the conversation, you might have noticed that in the MUP intercept, we have some words attributable to General Mladic which don't appear in the Croatian intercept, and I can refer you to the comment made by General Mladic in basically the second line of the SDB intercept, where we can see General Briquemont says: "I got through to General Tolimir this morning, so I suppose that he told you what the two of us had talked about." And you can see that line in lines 4 and 5 of the Croatian intercept on the left. And then you see the letter "M" in that intercept, followed by "...," but in the SDB intercept we'll see an actual answer, which says: "I'm listening." And then the conversation continues, and he says: "I told General Tolimir this morning that the Sarajevo sector was in a difficult situation ..." And so on and so forth. Did you consider those kinds of differences, the fact that one side could be heard and another -- in one intercept, and perhaps not as well in the other, as bearing significantly on the reliability of the intercept that we're looking at now, the Croatian intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I considered these problems which occurred at the time, and we can also see in the Croatian intercept that there is a note that the sound quality was poor. And due to these facts, I would say it's quite possible that one receiver heard the same conversation better than the other, so and that might explain why those differences occur in these two different intercepts, because they were intercepted from the two different locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you consider -- and we can see here a specific reference to the convoy number that was subject to approval. Here, we can see in the Croatian intercept it is "10-139/11," and you can see that precise number right in the middle of the SDB intercept as well. And we can also see that in the conversation, there's a reference in it that General Tolimir promised that General Briquemont would receive a reply between 1900 and 2000 hours "tonight." And you can see that also reflected in the Croatian intercept, where it says: "General Tolimir promised that I would receive the answer tonight between 1900 and 2000 hours." Did you consider that, in terms of, I would say, assessing the reliability of this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And we can see here that this information -- these numbers in both intercepts are the same, so both intercept operators from both sides, they could hear exactly what they've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender both of these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that there are no objections by the Defence. Both documents have a translation, and they are in the list -- the 65 ter exhibit list. They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 5544 shall be assigned Exhibit P2452, and 65 ter document 5612 shall be assigned Exhibit P2453. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move to the next tab. It will be tab 6 before the Trial Chamber, and I'd like to have, in e-court, shown to the witness, please, 65 ter 5547.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, have you had an opportunity to review this intercept? It's dated 30 March 1995 and timed at 0915 hours.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us about it and whether or not you were able to find any corroborating information supporting the reliability of the content of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an intercept about the conversation between a certain Aleksandar Radovic, and in brackets we can see it's from United States, "(USA)" - I assume this is United States - who is informing General Tolimir about the intelligence he received regarding the situation on the ground in Bosnia, so -- and, yes, I could find a corroborative document, which is the intelligence report of the VRS Main Staff, signed by General Tolimir on this same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could have, I'm sorry, P -- no, D237 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, Mr. Janc, can you tell us is this the document that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where in this document were you able to find support for the content -- rather, the reliability of the content in the Croatian intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the beginning of the second paragraph on the B/C/S and the second page in English, where we have a second paragraph, the beginning of the second paragraph, first sentence, where it says: "According to information from reliable sources, the Americans are providing the Muslims intelligence on VRS units." So -- and my conclusion is that this information -- or this intelligence report was derived from that intercept. From the information we can see in the intercept, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can see, on the first page of this report, that it appears to be dated on the 31st of March, although it's handwritten in one part and typewritten in the other. This is the B/C/S version I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it looks like "31st," yes, so it's the day after the conversation. My impression was it was the same date, because we can clearly see the number "1" after number "3."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does that make any difference to you, in terms of its relationship or impact on the reliability of the intercept that you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really, because this same intelligence report was compiled the day after, if it is, indeed, the 31st, which I believe it is, but it still contains the information, what has been discussing in the conversation from the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I'd like to tender the intercept. I see the intelligence report is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see an objection by the Defence. This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 5547 shall be assigned Exhibit P2454. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, behind tab 6 we have one last page, dated 30th of June, 1995, in draft translation. Is that correct? Does it relate to anything under this tab or is it put there by mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should be a mistake if it's -- yes, it should be a mistake. It should only be a document -- the last page of that tab should be a document with an ERN ending 0370-9043. If it's not that, then it's definitely an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's a short translation with the ERN number 0415 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see what you have. Yes, it's a mistake. It should go actually under tab 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's the first page -- should be the first page under tab 7, so I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We are actually going to tab 7 now, so if we could have, please, in e-court 65 ter 5549, and this will be the 30 June 1995 intercept. It has a time of 10.38. And I see we have the English in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Janc, have you had an opportunity to review this intercept as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about it, in terms of any corroborating or supporting information you may have reviewed concerning it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- there is information in this intercept, actually, which says that at the time, General Tolimir is standing in for General Mladic, and I could find a kind of document which is -- where it is written, actually, the same, that General Tolimir is standing in for General Mladic. But the problem with that document was and is that it is actually from the same source, which I mean the Croatian government, so -- and because in that document, and this is actually the intelligence report from the Croatian government, or intelligence administration of Croatian military forces, the problem is that you can't say if the information which is in this intercept was used for the report or the intercept corroborates the report, itself. We will see that in the report, there is much more information in relation to why General Tolimir is standing in at that time for General Mladic, and so I would say it's -- for my purposes, I couldn't actually figure it out, what corroborates what in this respect, because I was not able to definitely conclude that intercept is corroborated by other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you mean by that that it's corroborated by an independent source?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, I was referring to independent source.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at this intelligence report. It's 65 ter 7450. Mr. President, this is a document that wasn't originally on the Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc -- we'll wait for the English translation to come up. But is this the document that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, this document, dated 1st of July 1995, is the intelligence report I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can go to the last page of the document, we can see here that it is signed by Admiral Domazet, or type-signed, I should say. And then we can see the individuals and agencies it is delivered to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that includes a number of -- well, a number of individuals and agencies, as we can see. Now, if we go back to item number 2 in this document, it should be just one page back in the B/C/S - yes, that's right - and we should be on page 3 in the English, is this the assessment of the situation in the Main Staff of the VRS that you were referring to concerning the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, this first paragraph under item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there was more information here concerning the circumstances under which General Tolimir was standing in for General Mladic at the time. Can you just tell us what that is, specifically?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see from this paragraph that General Ratko Mladic went to Belgrade to the Military Medical Academy because of his health problems with kidneys, and that's why General Tolimir is standing in, based on this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned this information isn't in the intercept in question. How does that figure in terms of the information that's provided by -- or provided in the intercept? How do you view that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned, here we have more information than in intercept, itself, because in intercept we can just see that General Tolimir is standing in at the time already, and it is difficult to say what was the basis for this information in this intelligence report. Was it intercept, itself, or some other independent source? But, in any case, both the intercept and this information are pointing at the same thing, that General Tolimir is standing in, in absence of General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does the fact that this intelligence report was circulated so widely to numerous agencies and individuals in the Croatian military, apparently, does it suggest to you that it might contain information that is -- that has been vetted and is otherwise reliable?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would assume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I welcome Mr. Janc. I wish that this day will finish in keeping with God's will, not mine. A moment ago, Mr. Janc said that he can only confirm this information with the information provided by the government in Zagreb, that he has no other paper, and now Mr. Vanderpuye is trying to prove that Tolimir was deputy commander based on questions that are just rephrased in another form. Can something emanating from Croatia be evidence that Tolimir was deputy commander? I believe this is an attempt to prove something that is not contained in the documents, and I would appreciate clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a fair comment, but I think Mr. Vanderpuye will try to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first, I would simply say I'm not trying to prove anything. I'm not trying to prove that General Tolimir was a commander, deputy commander, or anything. The purpose of this is to establish or provide evidence of the reliability of the intercepts in question. With respect to what is said in the intercepts, the information in the report, as Mr. Janc has testified, sheds more light on what's contained in the intercept, particularly in light of General Tolimir's role, as it's recounted in the intercept, and we can all see that on the screen. And it doesn't say anything about General Tolimir being a deputy commander. What it says in the report is that during a trip to Belgrade, a medical check-up is scheduled at the Military Medical Academy because of Mladic's health issues with kidneys, and that during Mladic's absence, he will be replaced by General Tolimir, chief of security of the Main Staff of the VRS. And that's all it says, and that's all I'm saying, because I can't say more than what it says. So I hope that clarifies the issue for General Tolimir and for the Court, and if there are any questions regarding it, but that's -- that's the beginning and the end of the issue, in terms of what the evidence shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both documents, the intercept and this document, are from a Croatian source?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Both are from Croatian sources, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. With that said, Mr. President, I would tender these documents for admission; that is, 65 ter 5549 and 7450.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that there is no objection to add 65 ter 7450 to the 65 ter exhibit list and to the admission of these two documents. They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5549 shall be assigned Exhibit P2455, and 65 ter document 7450 shall be assigned Exhibit P2456. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to take the Trial Chamber to tab 8, and hopefully you'll find, under that tab, 65 ter 5559. It's -- oops, I'm mistaken, I'm mistaken. Just a moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. 5559. If we could have that displayed in e-court, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, we have an intercept here now, Mr. Janc. It's 30 July, 1995, and the time is 1950 hours. Have you had a chance to look at this one?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about it, in terms of your assessment of its reliability?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see from this intercept that it contains information that General Tolimir is ordered to go to Grahovo-Glamoc front on that day. And I think we don't have any clear document evidence to prove that he was going to this area on this day, but from -- from the investigation and especially from witnesses we interviewed, we know that he was going to that front -- to that area, part of the Bosnia and Herzegovina, around the end of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to look at any other Croatian-source material to see if there was consistent information, at least, with that -- with what's contained in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Again, we have the same issue as with the intercept before. We have the Croatian intelligence report, which is actually saying the same thing, so and here I think in that report, in that intelligence report, it's written the same as we can see in the intercept, itself. So I assume that information from the intercept was used to what is written in intelligence report then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at this intelligence report. It's 65 ter 5827.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, let me ask you: As far as the intercept is concerned, is there an indication as to why General Tolimir would have been sent to Grahovo and Glamoc in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no information why he's ordered to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We've got here now this intelligence report. It says, "For 30 July 1995," and this is again a Croatian-sourced report. If we go to the last page of this report, we'll see again that it is type-signed "Rear Admiral Domazet" and sent to the same or similar agencies and individuals as the last one we saw. And then it provides information on a number of -- a number of corps. If we go to page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S, we'll see some information specific to Grahovo and Glamoc areas. Is this the information that you're referring to as concerns General Tolimir that we can see at the bottom of the screen in English?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, the last paragraph is talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in this paragraph, it says that: "... General Tolimir and General Djukic from the VRS Main Staff have been sent to the Grahovo-Glamoc front-line in order to consolidate the situation and undertake measures to consolidate the forces." And then it provides some other additional information which concerns General Milovanovic and Karadzic; yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there's certain information that you came across concerning the situation in Grahovo and Glamoc around that period of time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is the information that you found in this report and in the intercept consistent with the information revealed by the investigation, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. At that time in this area, Glamoc-Grahovo area, there is an operation from Croatia, I think, offensive from their side, and most of the VRS is deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- a short moment, please. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to follow up on an answer you've given at page 17, line 14 to 18. You have stated that: "... we don't have any clear document evidence to prove that he was going to this area on this day, but from the investigation and especially from witnesses we interviewed, we know that he was going to the front." Do you -- can you refer us to a specific witness or witnesses who testified as to that fact you referred to in this statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness I was having in mind was -- in mind was his driver, Mile Micic, who I interviewed a few years ago. And during that interview, he told us that they are going to that area with General Tolimir at the end of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was just consulting with Ms. Stewart. I think that his statement was actually admitted during the course of his testimony, and that may be helpful. I don't have the specific reference, obviously, the line and page number. It's D296, and perhaps it might be of help to the Trial Chamber. I would at this time tender these two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see any objection by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: They are 65 ter 5549 and 745 -- I've done that. 5559, sorry, and 5827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These two documents will be received then as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 5559 shall be assigned Exhibit P2457, and 65 ter document number 5827 shall be assigned Exhibit P2458. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to pull up 65 ter 5589 in e-court, please. And the Trial Chamber should be able to find this document under tab 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, just a clarification. Under tab 8, in the index in the binder, there is a reference to 65 ter 7458, under seal. You didn't use it, and it is not contained in the binder. I take it that you aren't using it and not tendering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I apologise, also, for the error in the index. Okay, I think we have 65 ter 5589 now in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this an -- first of all, have you seen this document before, Mr. Janc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to review it, in terms of its content, to establish its reliability or lack thereof?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed this intercept with a long conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What can you tell us about it, in terms of your efforts to find material or review material that either support or detract from its reliability?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the conversation between Mr. Budo Kosutic and General Zdravko Tolimir on 13 December 1995. And on this occasion when they were talking, this gentleman, Kosutic, was asking General Tolimir about certain documents in relation to the fall of Srebrenica and the Zepa enclaves, and specifically he was having in his hand already a kind of -- a kind of declaration or statement signed by different sides, including UNPROFOR in -- after the fall of Srebrenica. And later on, they have been also discussing issues in relation to the list of Zepa prisoners and also the events surrounding the fall of Zepa. So and in this regard, there is, indeed, this declaration from Srebrenica events, which was signed by the members of the UNPROFOR, so this is one document which corroborates this conversation. The other one is actually the agreement on disarmament of Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you point to us, if you could, where in this intercept we can find these references to the lists that you've referred to or these documents that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite at the beginning, regarding Srebrenica, we can see reference to Mr. Deronjic, where it says that Deronjic sent good information from Srebrenica. The report sent by UNPROFOR, the commander of the Dutch Staff and by the Muslims. So this is the reference in relation to that document I've been talking about. In relation to Zepa, later on we can see there is a discussion, I think on the page after this one, regarding some lists. I was not able to find any of those lists which have been -- they have been discussing, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we'll have to go to page 2 for this.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For -- in English, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the English.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at the top part of this document, where it starts with "T," so Tolimir is talking: "There is, for example, for Zepa, all civilians on the list are the ones who left in the buses in an organised way. These lists have been kept; one came to us, one went to the Muslims, one to UNPROFOR, et cetera." So I was looking for these lists in our records, but I couldn't find them. So but later on, if you go down, we can see towards the end "T" is even talking, well, the agreement on taking Zepa, so I think here they are discussing this agreement on Zepa disarmament.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to locate that disarmament agreement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's, I think, already part of evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at P735.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what we have on the screen now, Mr. Janc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is Agreement on the Disarmament of the Able-Bodied Population in the Zepa Enclave, dated --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this the document you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, this is the document I was referring to, which is dated 24 of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P628. I think the B/C/S of this document you can find at page -- perhaps page 3. Anyway, it's the next page, ERN ending 110. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Janc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it as?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a declaration dated 17 July 1995, signed by the representatives of Muslims, UNPROFOR, and Miroslav Deronjic, which I have been talking about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that the reference to the "good information from Srebrenica that we could use" that's contained in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I'd like to tender 65 ter 5589.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, I don't see any objection. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask Mr. Vanderpuye to clarify with the witness [indiscernible] this information is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We didn't understand the full objection. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye asked the witness, Were you referring to this document when you were talking about good information? I would like to know what this "good information" is and whether Tolimir is mentioned in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I've understood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I've understood the nature of the objection. The "good information," for the benefit of Mr. Tolimir, is a reference to what's actually stated in the intercept, so perhaps we can pull that up. It's 65 ter 5589, and I'll point to precisely where it says so in the intercept, which will hopefully clarify the matter. In the third line in the intercept, you will see where it says "T," and then it says: "Da," "Yes," and then you will see it says "K," and then it starts with "Deronjic." And it says: "Deronjic sent me some good information from Srebrenica," that's the "good information" I'm referring to, "that we could use. The report signed by UNPROFOR, by the commander of the Dutch Staff, by the Muslims and by our," and it's in brackets, "(commander)," "that the entire process, everything that happened in Srebrenica was in accordance with the Geneva Conventions and all the rest." So that's the reference that I've made in my question to Mr. Janc in the context of the 17 July statement, which if we go back to, at P628, we'll see that it says: "During the evacuation, there were no incidents on either of the sides, and the Serb side has adhered to all the regulations of the Geneva Conventions, the International War Law ..." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This part Mr. Vanderpuye has read into the transcript was to be seen - now it disappeared - on line 4 and the following lines of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. And the latter part, relating to P628, you can see I've read from the bottom of the text in the English, which is on the left of the screen now. We should be on page -- on the second page of the B/C/S, in the last paragraph just above the signatures, and that refers to the Geneva Conventions, and the absence of any incidents, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope that that was helpful for you, Mr. Tolimir. The document will be received, 65 ter 5589.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document number 5589 shall be assigned Exhibit P2459. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to take to you tab 10, and the intercept is 65 ter 5598. If we could have that in e-court, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, have you had an opportunity to look at this -- this intercept as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, in our binders, at least in my binder, I don't find the English translation. We only have the B/C/S version, not the English one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I suspect, Mr. President, that it's quite possible it's the last page of your tab 9. I think I may have inadvertently put it there. But if it's not there, we do have it in e-court, in any event. But I suspect that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, you're right. I found it, last page at tab 9. It should be the first page of tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Again, I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I found it. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of this intercept, Mr. Janc -- well, let me put on the record that it's 27th of January, 1997, at 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of this intercept, were you able to find any information that corroborates the contents of it, bearing on its reliability, of course?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It's about the meeting which the president of RS at that time, Biljana Plavsic, organised. It was actually a farewell ceremony in Banja Luka for 17 retiring generals of the VRS. And at the end of the intercept, we can see who those generals are, and one of those being Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to confirm the information concerning the retirement of General Tolimir on or about that date?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. We have a document from President Biljana Plavsic, dated the day after this intercept, 28th of January, 1997, relieving General Tolimir from his duty as of 31st of January, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at 65 ter 4104. Do we not have an English translation? We don't. All right. I think there is a draft one, perhaps, in the tabs that I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have it in our binder, but perhaps it was not up-loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, can you -- first of all, can you confirm that this is the document that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I can't remember. Are you able to read Cyrillic, because it might be helpful to read into the record, at least, the part of this document indicating when General Tolimir's retirement is effective and, obviously, indicating his name.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read, but not as good as I would like to. In any case, there is an English translation of this one. But it says, at the last sentence -- in last sentence of this document, that General Tolimir is relieved from the duty as of 31st of January, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And we can see here, just for the record, at least, that the document number is 01-82/97, and dated "28.01.1997," and General Tolimir's name is indicated under item 1; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: "Date of birth: 27 November 1948"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. President, I would like to tender this -- both of these documents, 5598 and 4104 respectively. I think the 4104 would have to be marked for identification, pending the up-loading of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's possible to up-load it now and to submit it to the Registry. I have no idea. But first, Mr. Tolimir -- yes, I saw it. Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. For the sake of the record, it should be said that this is not a document on retirement. It says, quite clearly, he is relieved of his duty and put at the disposal of the Yugoslav Army, so this should be stated for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have the B/C/S version of the document, and this is the original one in front of us. Do you have any objection to the request of the Prosecution to tender it? I don't see any objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Mr. President. I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 65 ter 5598 will be received as an exhibit. 65 ter 4104 will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 5598 shall be assigned Exhibit P2460, and 65 ter document number 4104 shall be assigned Exhibit P2461, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a number of intercepts - I think I may have mentioned this to Mr. Gajic - relating to General Tolimir -- General Tolimir's involvement with matters pertaining to the Dayton Accords, which I can show to Mr. Janc, but I would submit that there's a sufficient-enough basis in the record of these proceedings, both in terms of the evidence the Trial Chamber has previously received pursuant to PW-70 concerning the authenticity of these intercepts as well as based upon Mr. Janc's testimony, that I would submit -- I would like to tender those documents directly. I don't know if Mr. Gajic or Mr. Tolimir has an objection to that at this point or if the Trial Chamber would prefer that I show each of them to Mr. Janc, but I think the relevance of the document is clear, on its face, and in light of the prior evidence in the case, I think there's a sufficient-enough basis to do what I will apply to do. So I can identify them, and perhaps that will assist Mr. Gajic or General Tolimir if there is any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that would be the first step, that you identify them and explain that, if all of them are included in your exhibit list we have received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. They are on the exhibit list. They are: 65 ter 5568, which is an intercept from 3 November 1995, and it's an intercept between General Tolimir and General Mladic concerning the developments in Ohio, where Dayton is; the next is an intercept which is 65 ter 5570, which is 7 November 1995, and this one involves General Tolimir and General Mladic, again from Dayton; and then we have another one which is 65 ter 5573, which is 18 November 1995, which concerns the disposition of a document that General Tolimir is talking about, which again concerns the same issues; and then we have 65 ter 5579, which is another intercept involving General Tolimir, Karadzic, which discusses the developments at Dayton again; and then we have 65 ter 5580, which is dated 21 November 1995, again on the same issues; and, lastly, we have 65 ter 5582, which, of course, is another conversation concerning the developments at Dayton. I know that General Tolimir has actually raised his involvement with the Dayton negotiations with a number of witnesses. The one that comes to mind is -- I believe it was Milenko Todorovic, the security chief at the East Bosnia Corps, and that came up in the context of some discussion about his work to prepare for the Dayton Accords or negotiations and the period of time that he was there, but I know that he's also raised that with some other witnesses. So I don't anticipate that there's any real dispute concerning it, but I would invite General Tolimir, if he has any objection to the admission of these intercepts, to say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I take it you have mentioned six documents. Is that correct, not to have any misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Yes, I've mentioned six documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you may recall that yesterday, before Mr. Janc began testifying, I raised the issue of intercepts marked by Witness PW-070, if I'm correct, and Mr. Vanderpuye said he would be using only the documents in this binder which was disclosed to us. So after this piece of information, I did not consider it an urgent matter to discuss these documents with General Tolimir. Could we, therefore, delay this question until a later time? Unfortunately, I did not bring the binder with me today, as Mr. Vanderpuye said that he might be using these documents at a later stage of the proceedings, either with this witness or some other witness, so we are unable to answer the question right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is a fair proposal, Mr. Vanderpuye, to prepare such response by the Defence and a possible decision by the Chamber. Could you briefly tell us the relevance of these six documents, these six intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I can tell you in a nutshell that the relevance of the documents has to do with: One, where is General Tolimir in the relevant period of time? That's the first thing. The second thing is it has to do with his continued contacts with other members of the -- of the Supreme Command and, obviously, of his command. He's in contact with President Karadzic directly in telephone -- on the telephone in some of these intercepts. He's also in contact directly with General Mladic. Both of these individuals, as you will know, are members of the alleged JCE in this case, and, therefore, his contacts with them, in terms of the importance of his role in Dayton, his importance -- the importance of his role in the Command of the VRS, as a member of the Command of the VRS, and his contacts and dealings with President Karadzic are, I think, of fundamental importance to the case. You'll remember that the order that -- for the troops to enter into Srebrenica, to begin with, is passed through General Tolimir from President Karadzic, so it's obviously that relationship is important, as is his relationship to General Mladic. And so what this shows, fundamentally, is that he is an important figure in all of this, and so on that very basic basis, it is relevant. It's also directly relevant to the issues that he, himself, has raised during the course of cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses. I'm not -- I can't remember exactly what I said yesterday, to be fair to Mr. Gajic, but I thought I said that all the intercepts I wanted to tender were on my exhibit list, I think. But maybe I said they were in my -- maybe I said they were in the packet. But in any event, it doesn't matter. I think if he wants to frame an appropriate response to the application, I certainly would invite that. I have no problem with it. But I do want to emphasise that we're not just simply putting in all of the intercepts that were authenticated by PW-070 during the course of his testimony; rather, we have a very limited number of them that we seek to admit. So it shouldn't -- it shouldn't entail Mr. Gajic having to go through all of the 74; simply the ones that are on the exhibit list, and that should do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I noted that these six intercepts are all from November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it's a good proposal to delay such a decision on admission of these six intercepts, and we wait for your response, Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic. You may continue, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just would like to show the witness 65 ter 5557.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I thought you would conclude now your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is one document that I want to show him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- and then that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a document from 12 July 1995. It's timed at 8.27. And have you had a chance to look at this particular document, Mr. Janc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to find corroboration -- or documentary corroboration, I should say, with respect to its content?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no direct document we have in relation to this intercept. But what is coming out of the intercept, itself, we can say that this is what was going on at the time, so the attack on Srebrenica enclave has already started at that time, I think. Yeah, it's self [indiscernible]. Of course, it was already concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Based on the investigation -- the information that you had at your disposal, are you able to determine at all whether or not the contents of this intercept is consistent with that information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, because we know that there was a NATO attack -- Air Force attack on Serbs near Srebrenica when they were advancing towards Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And to that extent, do you consider this intercept -- that is, the content of the intercept reliable or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on this information, yes, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I would offer this last intercept into evidence. And with that, that would conclude my direct examination of Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your position on the admission of this document? Do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5557 shall be assigned Exhibit P2462.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our first break now. After the break, Mr. Tolimir should commence his cross-examination. We will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I owe you an apology. By mistake, one of the pages of the list of exhibits that the Prosecution would be using was printed on both sides. We, Mr. Tolimir and I, have reviewed now this documentation. We will not be objecting to their admission, and that includes the documents Mr. Vanderpuye used at the end of the last session. I think it is to be expected that the Defence will not agree with the arguments presented by the Prosecution, and it will be up to the Chamber to decide about the relevance, whether the documents are probative, what they corroborate, what they do not corroborate. In any case, the position of the Defence is that these documents cannot be used to corroborate the Prosecution case about the existence of any kind of joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Gajic did mention that to me just before this session. I just wanted to point out to the Trial Chamber two things. The first is that I did find the reference to my representation yesterday that I'd be tendering these intercepts with respect to what was indicated on my exhibit list, rather than in the packets, just as a point of clarification. The second thing is notwithstanding the Defence arguments concerning the use of the material, I would point out to the Trial Chamber this evidence -- it is our view this evidence would be admissible, in any event, just based on the testimony -- or the prior testimony we have received in the record concerning this material. I can tell you more about it, but we'd have to go into private session to do that, but I think the Trial Chamber quite recalls the testimony of PW-070. And our view is that, in addition to that, the evidence that's provided by Mr. Janc obviously goes to the reliability and the strength of the intercept material, and that's how we intend to proceed with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have postponed a decision on that, and we would like to review the documents before we make a decision. Mr. Tolimir, you may now commence your cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet everyone present once again, and I hope that this day of trial will end in keeping with God's will, not my will. I welcome Mr. Janc. I hope his stay with us will be pleasant. And if we speak the same language, I will appreciate it if we make a pause between question and answer to avoid overlapping. May I ask the electronic courtroom to show the first document, 05536, the first document introduced through this witness. 05536. I'm sorry, I haven't written down the new exhibit number it received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This now P2438.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If we look at this document, P2438, and what is written there, and all the documents written in this way, without indication of who is saying what, could you tell us whether these documents of this kind and such intercepts are really intercepts or, rather, observations of those who were intercepting concerning the discussion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say these are observations. I would rather qualify them as the summaries of the intercepted communications, because, in my view, observations would look something differently. You know, you would perhaps have bullet points, you know, of observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please answer strictly the question asked. Is it possible to see, from these summaries of intercepts, to see what the interlocutors were actually saying and who said what exactly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From some of those, we can -- we can say that, yes, we can see that and we can conclude that. From this particular one, it's not that easy, who was saying what.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. From this and similar conversations that are summaries and not a transcript, can we see that they also reflect liberal interpretations made by people who were intercepting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to confirm that, we would need the actual intercept, itself, the transcript of intercept, what was said exactly by each individual in this conversation, and then we could say, you know, if everything what is part of this summary was, indeed, said within this conversation or something was added by intercept operator as their comment or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have those transcripts to present to the Chamber so that they can decide, themselves, rather than leaving it to the witness or the accused?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't have, in relation to these Croatian intercepts. This is all we have received from the authorities of Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that intercept operators and listening services are prohibited from re-telling or making their own accounts or making their own personal comments on the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I would agree with you, of course, but it is always important, what is written in the rules, how they should intercept the communication. So it depends on their rules. But, yeah, in general terms, I would agree with you, yes, nothing should be added by the intercept operators in the transcript or in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you and I shared the same profession in the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, can you tell me if you know that this method of summarising, as you called it, is a police method, not a method normally used by eavesdropping services?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say only what I know regarding as police work because I, for the whole of my life, I have been working with police and have been not involved in what army has been doing. So but for police work, I can say yes. Also, those summaries are quite common, as well as the actual transcripts, so for military I can't be precise because I have not been dealing with military.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Please, would you tell us, is it possible, when summarising the contents of a conversation, to express your own opinion, if you are an intercept operator, and to show one interlocutor what the other interlocutor said, or to make mistakes in identifying the speakers, or because of poor audibility, or for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when you are summarising, it's quite possible that you mixed someone, the interlocutors, so it's possible that mistakes happens. But in relation to what was said, I'm sure that the content of the conversation is there, regardless of, perhaps, the confusion, who said something. So I would say from my experience, because I've been involved also in this -- such work, that this can happen sometimes, because from the intercept operator's point of view, it might be very easy and understandable at the time when he is doing this work, but someone else who is reading the stuff later on might be confused with the formulation of the sentence or the summary. So that's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said a moment ago that these summaries were a common practice in the work of the police in their records of various activities, my question would be: Would you and I have been able to present to the courts in the former Yugoslavia such summaries and observations for court purposes, or were we allowed only to present transcripts to the Court, whereas we used summaries only for our own work in preparing cases for the Court?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would be talking about my experience, which not necessarily is the same for the whole former Yugoslavia. But for my country, it was possible to present only summaries to the Court. But the situation was a little bit different, because not only summary was enough. Of course, we have had the supported audio files always for each and every single conversation. It was just in case if someone was not understandable within the summary, then the audio would be used and released and transcribed, or at some point perhaps something was not important and became important later on, then instead of summary, the transcription of the actual conversation was done. So it's a little bit different situation, because, yeah, in order to present something in court, you would need the exact conversation recorded. But in this case, we don't have the audios, the actual recordings of the intercepted conversation -- conversations. This is the document we received in a shape it is. We are using it here in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible to make a judgement based on a police file or is forensic documentation necessary to convict someone of a crime? Is it necessary to catch the perpetrator in flagrante delecto or is it enough simply to intercept an incriminating conversation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say you have to -- you have to prove your case beyond reasonable doubt, and what evidence is enough might be -- might vary between different cases between different countries, and how to prove a certain case might be very different in different situations. So not one answer would be the perfect one for your question. I would say it depends on the situation, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Following up on your answer: Were these police reports of assistance to the Court only in forming a general opinion about the accused, in absence of other documents and evidence documenting the specific criminal activity? In other words, were police reports a sufficient piece of evidence for making a judgement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you're, again, now referring to what I experienced, I would say it depends on the case, again, and each of those intercepted conversations would be supported by audios, actual recordings of the conversation, itself, and also with other evidence which corroborated the intercept, itself. And, yeah, in order to put the case together, you would need much more evidence and then such a summary of some conversation. In some instances, in some cases, only the intercepted conversation would be the evidence enough to convict someone, so it depends on the case -- case-by-case situation, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since all my questions pertain to the period of the war and the period before the war, when the former SFRY laws were valid, and which are still relevant to judgements, do you remember that the activities of Martin Spegelj in importing weapons by Kikas [phoen] aeroplane and inciting soldiers to kill Serbs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir repeat the end of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters asked you to repeat the last part of your question. They didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, did you see the film in which the army documented that General Martin Spegelj, ex-commander of the Croatian Army, used an aeroplane called Kikas to import weapons without the approval of the central authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that he incited soldiers to kill Serbs by stabbing them in the stomach? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I watched this film, but it should be a long, long time ago, because these names are familiar to me, but the incident, itself, and the film, itself, not very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that the Presidency of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at that time in 1991, when this activity took place, decided that these police films cannot be used as adequate evidence against General Spegelj and they were not sufficient to take any measures? Maybe I should add: Do you remember that it was said in the communique that the police films were insufficient, inadequate; those were the words used?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no recollection of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't remember that in other republics of the SFRY, police documentation was useful only to the police and the Prosecutor's Office, not the Court, tell me, do you know of any country in Europe whose legislation includes a provision that a conviction can be made just on the basis of police documents or transcripts?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not easy to answer because, you know, it's not obvious, what do you mean by "police documents"? So when you say "transcripts," I guess, you know, you would be referring to the intercepted conversations of some communications. And, yes, those are. I mean, I think all police forces within Europe are using these means to prove the criminal activities of criminals. It's quite common in Europe, and it's totally legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us about any law to that effect, when these laws were passed, and since when such documents and such police methods are enough to bring in a conviction?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it depends on the country. But if you look into the former Yugoslavia, I think that police intercepting has been ongoing since, I think, 1993, 1994, at least in my country. Also, before there has been interception, but for different purposes; not to prove something in front of Court, but more for intelligence purposes. So but from the police point of view, you know, the real interception activities started, yeah, 15 years ago, perhaps, in the area of former Yugoslavia, and it was in accordance to the law, and it was accepted by Courts, you know, several times that it is total legally and not against any -- any human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it possible to conduct interception only on court orders, and were intercepts acceptable as evidence in court?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, again, I think, different in every country. So it depends on their Constitution, their legislation. You would find different -- different regulations regarding these activities. So for former Yugoslavia, it was a developing process. A long time before, at the beginnings, when they started with these activities, I think it was a kind of chief of department of certain administration approval enough to intercept someone, some activities. Later on, it developed. Of course, because of human rights, only court order can approve such interception, so -- and this is what is now common practice in all of our countries. Only Court can order any interception within the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you know that services for anti-electronic activities engage in disinformation and misinformation to gain advantage in combat?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this is more your area of knowledge than mine, but, yeah, yeah, it's possible, it's possible this is also going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, I would like to ask you: Can it be a relevant piece of evidence in court to use intercepts made by an enemy in war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Why not? Any piece of evidence, any piece of paper, can sometime become an evidence in court, and also the transcripts of intercepted communication can be evidence, especially if these transcripts are corroborated with documents, what I have been presenting during my testimony today and yesterday. So the sole purpose of my testimony was to prove that the intercepted communication -- communications are reliable because some other independent document sources are -- are showing the same facts, or presenting, or are talking about the same issues, what is actually written in the intercept, itself. So I would say, yes, you can use such documents in court as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is a very interesting issue you are discussing with the witness. Only one observation. It will be, at the end of this trial, the duty of the Chamber to decide which kind of document can be used for any kind of judgement. There is, of course, we have to prove if there are reasons to rely on any of these documents. This is the normal duty of any trial chamber in the world. We are not bound by the answers of Mr. Janc, as he tries to provide you with his knowledge from the former Yugoslavia or other states in Europe. We will not rely on that because this is irrelevant for our own legal opinion we have to form at the end of the whole trial. Therefore, you should perhaps try to focus on those areas of his knowledge and his expertise as an investigator of the Prosecution. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, since you used to be an investigator dealing with the events from the war, would you say that intercepts made by the enemy side may be used as impartial evidence in court?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer would be the same as the one previous. Yes, it can be, especially if it can be corroborated by other independent sources. But as just the Presiding Judge explained at the end, it's always up to the Trial Chamber to decide on its reliability and admissibility and everything. So it's my duty to present as much corroborative evidence as possible, and at the end of the day it's up to the Trial Chamber to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. For example, the latest war, the one in Libya, at the beginning of the war there were only insurgents in Tripoli. Now there's an army. After this, can the evidence launched by one side against the other be reliable, can it be impartial? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not an appropriate question for this witness. He is an investigator of the OTP of this Tribunal, dealing and investigating facts of events in the former Yugoslavia, and he reviewed material documents and other things. You and I and Mr. Janc are able to read newspapers, and perhaps follow television, but it is absolutely irrelevant to hear the opinion of Mr. Janc in relation to events in Libya. You should focus on his expertise and the answers he can provide you with in relation to the events in the former Yugoslavia relevant to the indictment against you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let's look at 03928, which speaks of events from the former Yugoslavia, and this is a document tendered through this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now P2440.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 2 of this document. I will quote: "Through refugees we have confirmed the information that members of the Nordic Battalion of UNPROFOR in the area of the Tuzla region are organising and conducting the training of soldiers from the 2nd Corps of the so-called BH Army in tanks and armoured personnel carriers. Driver training is being conducted at the Poljice military training-ground, not far from Tuzla. UN sources state that after the training, combat vehicles of the UNPROFOR Nordic Battalion Command will be given to 2nd Corps units." My question is the following: As an investigator, did you pay attention to this piece of information concerning the illegal arming and training of one side in the conflict and the partial attitude of the UN towards the sides to the conflict while they were engaged in a peacekeeping mission? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During my work here for the OTP, I came across many of such information, and I reviewed, I think, most, if not all, of your intelligence information from that time.
