And in -- yes, if it was important for our case, for what you are charged with, I would also consider such information as some important, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this information important when one bears in mind that the BH Army planned joining up the central part of Bosnia with the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, and that they were helped in this by UNPROFOR? This is from the standpoint of these proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information, itself, it's interesting, but, you know, on the other hand, we have to know that this is your information, your intelligence, which is not necessarily correct. But for our case, I don't think this was of big interest. It is more information in interest for you, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an OTP investigator, did you find only the information provided by Muslims, even if only through intercepts, to be more interesting and relevant, in comparison to information provided by refugees? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. For Prosecution, all information are important, being from one or the other side engaged in the conflict. And we all know that we used, in this trial, many documents from VRS side, many documents from Muslim side and from UNPROFOR side, so many, many documents. So everything is very important, and I would not say, you know, something is more important than other -- or more reliable than other. So for each and every single piece of information, you have to assess it first, how important it is for your case, and then you can -- you can use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. Given your expertise in documentation, which I believe you gained by virtue of your position in the police of your country, maybe I should start with asking: What special skills do you possess with regard to handling documentation, by virtue of your position as a policeman in your country, and what country is this that you belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have been the member of the Slovenian police from 1993 onwards up until 2006, when I joined this Tribunal, and I have been trained -- my secondary -- I completed secondary police school, and later on also college for police and security studies, and also I graduated from the Criminal Investigations and obtained a specialist of criminal investigations title. So this is my qualification. And throughout these trainings and schools and studies, I've been involved in -- in these -- yeah, these issues how to also handle certain documentation which is obtained throughout the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. The second question I have is: Page 47, lines 16 to 20, your answer is: "The information, itself, is interesting, but, you know, on the other hand, we have to know that this is your information, your intelligence, which is not necessarily correct." Given your expertise, can you assist me to understand how you come to the conclusion that this particular intelligence is not necessarily correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I didn't mean, actually, that it's not correct. I was just speaking as hypothetically in this case, because it's not verified in this case. I would need more -- more time to take a look into -- into other documentation, if there is any corroborative documents which would say, yes, this is what happened at that time. So when I used the word "which is not necessarily correct," it was just hypothetically speaking that information, especially intelligence information, might not be always correct, especially when just a few minutes ago General Tolimir, himself, asked me if it is possible or if I know that it is common for intelligence services that some information must -- are misleading and intentionally misleading, in this sense I was thinking of when testifying about this might not necessarily be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want to ask a question to the witness. I wanted to ask a question to the Defence, to General Tolimir. I want to take advantage of this at this juncture, because I've been listening to the questions and answers between Judge Nyambe and the witness on possible false information provided by one party. General Tolimir, on page 44 of the transcript, lines 5 to 7, you asked the witness whether the anti-electronic activities services - what's the exact word in French - so the counter -- the electronic counter-intelligence services during activities can provide false information in order to gain combat advantage, and the witness said it was possible. Now, I'm taking the floor because what we are dealing with is a case, we're not dealing with theory, and the Prosecutor showed us a series of intercepts, so intercepted conversation. I would like to know how the Defence will organise its work regarding that particular issue. Is the Defence going to use this witness to tell us that such and such intercepts were fabricated to deceive, or will you call further witnesses to confirm this submission, because we're not dealing with a theory here. Actually, the President told you not to do so, and rightly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your position on that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Judge Mindua. I will not deny anything. Everything that the witness said during the examination-in-chief is to my advantage, because not a single document speaks of any activity of mine in combat. It says that in Dayton, I was part of a joint criminal enterprise. Were Hill and others also part of this enterprise? Then I have no need to prove anything. If the Court thinks that all those who attended Dayton were members of a joint criminal enterprise, I will be happy to be convicted of that. If the Dayton Accord or the Accord on Freedom of Movement, signed and proposed, actually, by UNPROFOR, are part of a joint criminal enterprise, I accept that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tolimir, I think that we're talking at cross-purposes, because you did say that some intercepts may have been fabricated, forged, to deceive the other party. Now, we have to make -- to have an opinion on the basis of those intercepts, and my question is: Will you provide evidence in order to make sure that these intercepts have no probative value? That's my question. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were asked by Judge Mindua. Is it possible for you to say something about it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President. I was waiting for you to finish conferring. The Defence does not need to prove anything. It needs to challenge the accusations by the OTP. That's what I'm trying to do. If I am being asked to prove what they are saying, I'm willing to do that. But it's not up to me to prove anything, but only to challenge what is being put here. Yesterday, I spoke about forgery. Look at 05542, admitted through this witness, when I said that this was a false document, it was forged by the OTP. Thank you. This is untrue, this document is untrue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, this is Exhibit P0446. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correction, Your Honour, P2446. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As I don't have the document, let me tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are considering the situation. Please wait.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, we can see a document here. I won't read it out. And it says that General M. Stanley sent an urgent message to General Tolimir, saying that aerial attacks would follow unless the shelling of the town of Bihac didn't stop, and General Tolimir denied, and so on. My question: Have you checked who General M. Stanley is and whether such a general, in fact, existed in Bosnia at the time of the war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, because of our conversation yesterday, I was able to check this name of this individual this morning. And I have to agree with you that this individual, he wasn't general at the time, but there was Mike Stanley who was a colonel at the time. And I was able to find that he was a member of British Army deployed in Sarajevo at the time, and actually he's a Serb by origin. He's also having one other Serb name, but I cannot remember it right now. So he existed at the time, and I think because of his knowledge of Serb language, that's why he was in contact with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you can't recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have now French in the English channel. That was a mistake. Please, again, your question. I think the interpreters will check that. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: As you can't recall, it escapes you at the moment, I'm asking you whether the man in question was perhaps Milan Stankovic, who was in UNPROFOR and who spoke the Serbian language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is the person, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he at the time of a lower rank than general and colonel, quite a lot lower? Was he some sort of Serb interpreter for General Rose? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, and I was not right when saying that he was a colonel at that time. He was actually a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you check whether the information provided by Tolimir, that the Muslims, themselves, were shelling Bihac, was it correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information couldn't be corroborated by any independent source, so I didn't find any corroborative documents regarding this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now look at -- again look at document P2440, page 2, which we had on the screen just a little while ago. Could we look at page 2, paragraph 4. I will quote from paragraph 4. It's the last page in English, just above the signature, the second paragraph before last. It says: "The conflicts between units of the 5th Corps of the so-called BH Army and the forces of the National Defence of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia continue, with no movements of the front-line. Members of the 5th Corps Command stress that they will resolve the problem with Fikret Abdic by negotiations, and that he will not be presented with an ultimatum to surrender to 5th Corps forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Were you aware that the Muslims in the Bihac pocket were at war with themselves? Some Muslims were attached to Fikret Abdic, and they were at war with the 5th Corps of the BH Army, and vice versa? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that I'm not very well aware of the situation in Bihac area, because for most of the time being here with the OTP, I've been dealing with Srebrenica investigations, so I wouldn't dare to say or comment much on what was going on in that part of the Bosnia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. I'm not sure if I'm maybe missing something, but the date of this document that General Tolimir is referring to seems to be from June 1994. The intercept which he's put his question is from October -- I'm sorry, September of 1994, so I'm not sure if the question that he's asked Mr. Janc concerning the Muslim activity in Bihac is related to events that transpired in June 1994 or in September 1994, to which the intercept speaks. I haven't seen anything that connects these two documents in the question, nor do I see that it arises from the context of the question that such an inference can be drawn. So perhaps General Tolimir can explain or elaborate, I suppose, on his question about whether or not the information contained in his report in June relates to the events that are in the intercept in September in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, a correction to the transcript. This is not a conversation from September, but 28th of June, 1996. It's written there. Bear that in mind. And, second, I used a quotation to show how long that conflict lasted, and now I would like to ask Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know how this -- how long this conflict lasted and when it ended?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to understand your response. Are you referring to the intercept of the 10th of September, where this so-called General Stanley is mentioned, or are you referring to another document, just to understand the different documents and events and dates? And I see here in the transcript, in your response: "This is not a conversation from September ... 1996." I think this must be another mistake. Please explain the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, this conversation that was allegedly intercepted, does it date back to September, the one where General Mike Simon -- or, rather, Milan Stankovic is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is dated 10 September 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And not 1996, as you stated, Mr. Tolimir. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I note, for the record, it's a conversation recorded on the 10th September 1994. P24664 [as interpreted]. We're talking now about 2446, page 2, paragraph 4, dealing with the origins of the conflict between Muslims in the Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question to Mr. Janc is this: Does he know whether this conflict lasted until the end of the war, and was it so fierce that it lasted more than a year?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same answer as before. I'm afraid I don't have enough knowledge to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Considering that this document was introduced through you, I used it as evidence because the Muslim conflict still went on at that time. Now, at that time when this conversation happened in 1994, was the conflict between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the forces under Fikret Abdic in the Bihac pocket still ongoing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on information we can see from the intercept, itself, we can conclude that, yes. And also from the information which are contained in these reports -- UNPROFOR reports, yes, the conflict was ongoing, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Janc. Could we now look at P2447. In English, it's page 2 in e-court, paragraph 3. There it is. It says -- it's the wrong document. I apologise to the e-court and to the Trial Chamber. My mistake. It's 2448, page 2, paragraph 3. Thank you, Aleksandar. Now the Trial Chamber can see this third paragraph. It says: "General Rose told Vice-President Ganic that the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot shell the Serbs and at the same time expect us to intervene."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: At this time, did General Rose confirm as well that Muslims wanted NATO to intervene against Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean by this, this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Does this document confirm - it's dated 10 September 1994 - that Muslims asked UNPROFOR that NATO should intervene against the Army of Republika Srpska in the Bihac pocket? That's also 10 September, the same date when this conversation was recorded.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's -- it confirms that NATO should intervene. But as I read it here, you know, that they were informed -- the NATO or UNPROFOR was informed, what was going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, in fact, I don't find the sentence you have read into the record. Where is --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it would be in the second complete paragraph, but third -- what is apparently the third paragraph down in the page, and it's the second -- third sentence of that paragraph. It's just about halfway through the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Because it was in a different way recorded, and therefore I asked, I would like to read it into the record. I quote: "General Rose has accordingly advised Vice-President Ganic that the government cannot shell the Serbs and at the same time expect us to intervene." Is this the relevant part of this document you were referring to, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That is the relevant passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my question to Mr. Janc is: Does this document confirm that the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina expected at the same time from General Rose that NATO would intervene? It's 10 September 1994, the date when I said they want to force NATO to intervene against Bosnian Serbs. Does this document confirm it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's written there, that -- what is expected from the UNPROFOR, so this is what they were most probably told at the time; I mean, the UNPROFOR was told by the Vice-President Ganic at the time. So this written there, so that's all I can comment on. But what steps have been taken by UNPROFOR later on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Please, does this transcript we're looking at, dated 10 September 1994, 2446 - if we could see it again, thank you, P2446 - the document we had before this one, is it coincidental that at the same time, demands are made for NATO intervention simultaneously with these intercepts, with very grand names given to interlocutors, making them look like generals, and is it proper evidence for a court?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, if it is proper evidence, I think it's up to the Trial Chamber, at the end, to decide and to put weight on these documents. But, yes, I can admit that Mr. Mike Stanley hasn't been a general at that time. He was captain, and this information in intercept is wrong. Why is it written "General," I can't say. Again, because we know this is a summary, perhaps it was a confusion of the intercept operator who has prepared this summary, or whoever prepared this summary, or something else I can't say. But the other information from the intercept, itself, has been corroborated by these documents, and this is what was going on at the time on the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you study the situation on the ground at the time, and do you know what the Muslims were demanding from NATO at the time and all the things they were doing to cause a NATO reaction against Serbs? Have you studied that? Is it something a researcher would do or is it something that is for the Trial Chamber to do?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that I haven't been studying the situation in Bihac at that time very extensively, because when preparing for this testimony, I've been mostly focusing on corroborative documents which might confirm or support this intercept. And in order to confirm the reliability of intercept, itself, I didn't go into deep details what was, indeed, going on on the ground at that time in that area. That would entail a lot of work, and I'm sure that other investigators who have been dealing with this particular area within the OTP have been studying these documents. But me, personally, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution called another witness here, who used to be a commander in Bihac, and asked absolutely no questions about this, although the person was very qualified to speak about it. It had to do with General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was: Does the witness know that General Milovanovic was here as a Prosecution witness and that he could have been asked about this issue? He was much more qualified than a researcher or an investigator, but nothing was asked of him.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that he was here and he testified, and I'm sure he was much more qualified to talk about the incidents and what was going in that area at the time than any researcher here from the OTP, because he was witnessing these events.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like e-court to now show P2452, to stop wasting time on this event described in two sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, when we look at P2452, it's again a transcript introduced through you. Please look at line 5, which begins with the words: "Tolimir." Tolimir said: "Sector Sarajevo ... due to the shortage of fuel ..." Et cetera, et cetera. My question is: Did you see in other transcripts that Tolimir said that, like you compared it to 2453, or perhaps someone else said that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the corroborative documents to this intercept is the other intercept from the BiH side, and we would need to take a look into that one, I think, to compare, perhaps, both of them and to check that. But I can take a look right now, having it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tolimir is right. It could be P2453, which is 65 ter 5612, behind tab 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask the electronic courtroom to show it below the text in Serbian or in English, if possible. If not, we should display it separately. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at line 4, please, where it says: "Brinkman: I told Tolimir this morning that Sarajevo was in a difficult situation ...," et cetera. Did such a transcript lead to confusion, ascribing certain words to one person, whereas they were actually uttered by another person? In other words, was something that Brinkman said ascribed to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Here we have a situation where we have such a problem, when we have two intercepts. One is the actual transcript, this the one which we see on the screen, and the other one is a summary. So and this can happen, which I testified before, when you're summarising something, that you put it down, something which is differently where what was actually said. So and here is one example. So we don't know, actually, which is -- which is correct now, because in both we have information that -- that was discussed, the problem with the fuel in Sarajevo Sector, but in one intercept we have that General Tolimir said that; in another one, that General Brinkman. So but this is the intercept. I'm referring now the Croatian one, the other one which is not on the screen now, where it is noted that the sound quality was poor, so and this might be part of the reason why someone didn't understand correctly what was being said during the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree with me that for whatever reason, because of whatever mistake, a summary may ascribe certain words to one interlocutor rather than the person who really said it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything is possible. We have also instances where actual transcripts of the intercepts were transcribed wrongly, so that interlocutors were wrong, actually, once this was assigned to another interlocutor involved. So there are such problems in these intercepts, but I would say not in all cases. You would find such problems in some of them, but not in all of them. It is normal, with this kind of work, that you also made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we need our second break now. We adjourn, and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are looking at this exhibit, look at where it says: "Translated from English." Can you explain why this is a translation into English from a Serbian text by a certain woman called Svetlana, who served as an interpreter for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that it is translated from English in intercept, itself, into Serbian, I would assume, or into B/C/S, and we've been discussing this issue yesterday. We have three of such intercepts where it says: "Translation from English," and they were all provided to the OTP by the SDB Sarajevo back in 2002. One of the reasons would be that conversation was going on partially in English and translated into B/C/S, and that's why, perhaps, this conversation was noted down initially in English, because we can see here, under number 1, that the conversation is going on with help of interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a Croatian intercept, or, rather, summary, and we see that this conversation was assisted by an interpreter. Was this interpreter with one interlocutor, since this was a telephone conversation, or was the interpreter present with both speakers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what we have on our screen is the BiH MUP SDB intercept, and not Croatian intercept. And as I understand, only one interpreter was involved, with the name Svetlana, which is not on this intercept which we have on our screen, but her name appears on the Croatian intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you proved this transcript on the screen using this Croatian text that indicates that the conversation took place with the assistance of Svetlana, the interpreter, can you tell us whether these two conversation were identical or is there a possibility that the interpreter was interpreting from English? Could it have gone into air in Serbian if it was a conversation that took place with the help of an interpreter who was speaking Serbian? Could it have gone into air -- on air in English?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logically, it would go into the air in Serbian language, because she is actually conducting conversation with the VRS side and she's communicating what is -- or translating what is said to her by General Brinkman in Serbian language to the VRS side. So it would be going through the air in Serbian language, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this, then, an intercept or something else, seeing that it took place with the assistance of an interpreter who was able to hear what the general was saying and was not going on air; I mean, what General Brinkman was saying?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, when you are talking over the phone and you have a conversation with interpreter present, you are discussing or you're having conversation in front of the telephone as well, so whatever you say perhaps in English is most probably also going through the air somehow, and what else the interpreter is interpreting back into English to you is also probably heard and going through the air somehow. So I can't say exactly what kind of intercept this is, but it's possible, because it was heard by both sides, Croatian side and BiH side, that it is a conversation going through the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, I need a clarification. Do you know anything about a person with the name Svetlana? Do you know the second name, do you know whether she was engaged to one of the sides of UNPROFOR, or do you know anything more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall her last name right now, but I'm quite sure that she worked for the UNPROFOR side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What conclusion would you draw from this information with respect to her position during this conversation? Was she present with General Brinkman or with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say she was present with General Brinkman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, what could be heard by the interlocutors -- no, by those who made the intercept? Which language could be heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most logically would be that, of course, the Serbian language would be heard going through the air. But if someone is conducting conversation and the other one is interpreting to him, also this part of conversation can be heard, what is going on. So I wouldn't exclude the possibility that what was said in English language by General Brinkman was also heard over the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Have you just expressed your assumptions or something you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is something I know, because we have, I think, audio -- let me explain just because why -- because I think we have audio records of the conversations between Gvero and General Nicolai, and I think we can hear both, and the station is the same. Svetlana is interpreting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that some transcripts were introduced here of conversations where you hear only the Serbian speaker, never anyone from the UNPROFOR Command? Could you explain why this is so?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we also have such situations when we also hear the Serbian speakers, and I don't know -- you know, it's more technical issues, I think, why at some point both sides can be heard and other situations only one side can be -- or only one interlocutor can be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Here is a conversation when you can hear both speakers, and what Brinkman is saying is related in Serbian, as is what General Mladic says. Would it be logical that any intercept operator would hear the English language and make a note that something is said and heard in English? Would it be proper to reflect that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it would be proper. And, you know, we don't know much -- enough about this particular conversation, why it was noted like that or why it says: "Translation from English." So there are several options, and I don't exclude the possibility that the original intercept has been transcribed in English just because, perhaps, only one side of the conversation can be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the two interlocutors are speaking in a room, and Svetlana is talking on the phone and relating only what Brinkman says, would it be logical to hear only Svetlana and her interlocutor, and if you are eavesdropping on the room, you would hear both ends of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, sometimes -- and we have those notes in intercepts that only one side can be heard. But in this specific situation, even if only one side was heard, and in this case I would say the UNPROFOR side, because you have interpreter involved in it, he would interpret everything what was said on the other side. And in this case, if you can hear what one side is saying, you would actually hear the whole conversation from both sides, because this would be interpreted back to the person who is involved in the conversation. And that's one of the reasons why, perhaps, this was transcribed in English and then translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you see that in this intercept, as you call it, General Mladic says, in line 3: "I'm listening." And then "M" says: "The convoy will be approved." And then in the third line from the bottom, he says: "You'll have it tomorrow." And in the last line, he says: "Good night." Were both interlocutors heard over the wire on the air? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most probably, but not necessarily, because what I just explained is that this, for example, "Good night" word might be translated in this intercept from the English translation of Interpreter Svetlana, so it is not necessary that the intercept operator heard General Mladic, itself. It's possible that he just heard the translation of what General Mladic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you are excluding the possibility that General Mladic was heard, you say that he heard only Svetlana and translated her, is it possible that the intercepting devices were in the room where Svetlana was having a conversation with the general in English, and that this is what was recorded and transcribed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the beginning of your question was a misstatement. Mr. Janc said - that was the last part of his answer - it's possible that he just heard the translation of what General Mladic said. Your representation was, I quote: "As you are excluding the possibility that General Mladic was heard ..." I don't see a foundation for this statement. Please phrase your questions carefully. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, for the sake of clarity: In this conversation, were both Svetlana and General Mladic heard? Can they both be heard? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this piece of information we have in front of us, meaning from this intercept, I can't conclude either way. So it can be that both were heard or only one was -- one side was heard involved in this conversation. So they are both options possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Janc, if both interlocutors were not heard, was this an intercept of a conversation or was it a monologue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is intercepted communications still, and it's not a monologue. It's just that only one side of -- involved in conversation can be heard, which is due to technical reasons, because the other side cannot be intercepted for some reason. I think that in front of this Trial Chamber, there were evidence and witnesses explaining why that happened, that only one side can be heard. And because of the involvement of the interpreter, I explained why is that -- is then also possible that you can hear actually what the other side was saying, because everything is interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, may I jump in and put a question. How is it possible to have such a record of a conversation, suggesting that two people, Mr. Mladic and Mr. Brinkman, are discussing, and at the end say, Good night, to each other, if only one side could be heard? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding would be that if initially this was transcribed in English, because it says: "Translation from English," everything what was said in English was transcribed, and most probably the translator/interpreter translated the word "good night" back to Mr. Brinkman, and that was what was heard, and it was noted as Mladic said that. That's my understanding, that this is possible, because sometimes you would put it like the other side was talking, regardless that that was interpreted to Mr. Brinkman. So from my point of view, a better transcript would be, actually, what was said by each person involved in a communication. If interpreter said something, I would put that interpreter said this and that or interpreted back what other person said during the conversation. But in a wartime period, when you have many of those conversations, perhaps this was not the important issue and they haven't put much -- much effort to do it in a proper way. So it's difficult -- it's difficult, actually, just based on this intercept, to decide whether both sides were heard during a conversation or only one. It's difficult for me to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, if - and I assume that was the case - Svetlana was together with General Brinkman during this conversation, and he helped to understand the words of Mladic and interpreted back to Mr. Mladic, assuming that either Mr. Brinkman or Svetlana was talking, can you exclude the possibility that both sides were to be heard, as written down here in this document, both sides? I'm referring to Mr. Mladic and Mr. Brinkman, or Svetlana interpreting for him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this cannot be excluded, so it's totally possible that both sides were heard during this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you exclude the possibility that only one side was heard by the intercept operator, only Mr. Mladic or the UNPROFOR side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's totally possible that only one side was heard during the conversation, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How is that possible, if you look at this document, where it is said that Mr. Brinkman, himself, or by the interpreter, Svetlana, said something, and then there is an answer by Mr. Mladic, and then again something which is supposed to have been said by Mr. Brinkman or Svetlana?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have to know that this is the translation from English, as it says. At the beginning, as part of this document, we have this notation, this is translation from English. And we know that General Mladic hasn't been responding in English, and in that case this is impossible that this conversation would take place in English between these two individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that the communication was in English. Looking at this document, I see that there are two sides communicating with requests and an answer, and another answer, and so on. If Svetlana was on the UNPROFOR side with Mr. Brinkman, I would assume it was in Serbian, the whole communication between Svetlana and Mr. Mladic. I just want to understand how it could be that you have a reference to both sides in this document if only one side was heard by the intercept operator.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that -- I am trying to explain this, because when she has been -- if only the UNPROFOR side was heard during the conversation, whatever was said by Mr. Mladic in B/C/S, this had been translated by Interpreter Svetlana in English into [sic] Brinkman, and on that occasion the intercept operator heard what was translated, and that's what he put down as being said by Mladic. That's my understanding, that this might be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I understand. Thank you very much. If you look at line 3 of this conversation, for the first time the line starts with "M," and then it is written there, I quote: "I am listening (X ...," who should be the interpreter, if you look three lines up, "... assumes that this is General Mladic)." Does this line support your last explanation of a possible way the intercept operators could catch the conversation, or what is your interpretation of this line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same, it might be, you know, translated, and what -- translated back to Mr. Brinkman by Interpreter Svetlana, what General Mladic said, and also she might add to that what she translated, that she assumes that this is General Mladic. So this, what is in brackets, I would say, is not what was said by General Mladic, but what was added by Interpreter Svetlana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, my apologies for the interruption, but I wanted to understand the understanding of Mr. Janc of this document. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. I was having some minor problems with my screen, but I have been assisted and now it's working.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says up here: "The MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina SDB." Can you explain to the Chamber what this means?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "MUP" is Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "SDB" is State Security Service, which is part of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, from your experience, did the State Security Service engage in eavesdropping? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did its Department 6 engage in bugging rooms or premises or intercepting radio waves? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of what exactly Department 6 is engaged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, did you ever wonder who this person, "NI277" was, whether that person could be identified, and whether it was this person who translated this from English?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that we talked to individual from that service who might identify this individual with number 277, but I'm not exactly sure if he asked this individual about this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As it can be seen in the document tendered here that it is a translation from English, can you tell us whether you are in the possession of the original from which this translation was made?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, this is all we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that the American intelligence service delivered the text in English and that it was then translated into B/C/S by the translator?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That would be speculation from my side. I don't have enough information to say either way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's look at P245 [as interpreted] admitted into evidence through your testimony and which you explained here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please give us the correct reference. It can't be P245.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have made an error when noting it down. It's 65 ter 05547. It's P2454. Thank you. Thank you, Aleksandar. Now we see the document. It's the document where: "Aleksandar Radovic of the US informed General Tolimir that they had reliable information that the BH Army was receiving information from satellite images which the Americans have been sending them."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is the following: Do you know whether the Americans delivered to UNPROFOR information arising from eavesdropping the warring parties? Did the Americans do this for UNPROFOR as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that pilotless aircraft were also responsible for gathering intelligence for electronic reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would assume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find any information to the effect that pilotless aircraft were conducting a reconnaissance of the territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly. I know that you have been reporting about those pilotless aircrafts within your reports very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that all UNPROFOR premises were under the surveillance of American intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at D48, please, page 28, and page 3 in Serbian. I do apologise. It's page 28, paragraph 3. Please look at the part underlined in red. Page 28, thank you. Thank you. It's on this first page that we see on the screen the part underlined in red ink. I quote: "The former UNPROFOR commander, Rose, claims in his memoirs that his former headquarters in Sarajevo was monitored by US services in 1994 and 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Is it possible that the English recorded the conversation in a room and that it was somehow delivered to the American security service, who translated the transcripts? I'm sorry, I said "the English," but I should have said "the Americans."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document should not be broadcast. I was told it is confidential, which is a surprise for me. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's a great surprise for me as well, because this is a public document which we have used more than once in this courtroom, and I think there is no obstacle to its being used as a public document. If I recall correctly, and this can be checked, it was used with a protected witness, but it's only where this witness worked and the name of the witness that are confidential and that is confidential in the transcript, but this document should be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Registrar is in agreement with that. Yes, it may be broadcast. Please continue. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I see that it's time, just about, for the break. I just wondered if we could have an estimate from General Tolimir as to how much longer he anticipates to go with Mr. Janc so that we know when to have Mr. Butler available to testify as the next witness. That's all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We're planning to finish in the course of the first session, and I believe that this will be within the time that we envisaged for the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no doubt that you have approximately one and a half hours left. It's only the question if we start first with Mr. Butler and continue with the cross-examination of Mr. Janc, as he will be available at any time, as an investigator of this, or is it better to continue and finish with Mr. Janc. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It would be better to finish with Mr. Janc for all time, I think. I may have a brief redirect just to clarify some issues, but I think it's better to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, in the afternoon, at 2.15 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of July, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
